11740:
The verb to parody means to imitate something — a person, a style, a song, a movie, a speech, or really anything recognizable — in a deliberately exaggerated and comic way, so that the imitation makes people laugh, and often makes a quiet but pointed comment in the process.

The idea at the heart of parodying is this: you study the original closely, identify its most distinctive features, and then amplify those features to an absurd or comic extreme. The result is something that is clearly based on the original, but is stretched, twisted, or inflated just enough to become funny.
The Three Things That Make It a Parody

Three elements need to work together: you imitate the original closely enough that people recognize what you're copying, you exaggerate its most distinctive features, and the result is humorous. Remove any one of these, and it stops being a parody. If you just copy something faithfully, that's plain imitation. If you exaggerate without resembling the original at all, that's just being random or silly. But when you do both together — copy recognizably and exaggerate comically — you are parodying.

Imagine a well-known politician who always waves their hands dramatically when they speak, uses unnecessarily complicated vocabulary, and loves to say "let me be absolutely clear" before everything. Now imagine a comedian on stage who waves their arms wildly, uses absurdly long words for simple things ("I am now in the process of consuming a liquid beverage" instead of "I'm drinking water"), and says "let me be absolutely, completely, unambiguously, utterly, and irrefutably clear" before every single sentence. That comedian is parodying the politician.

The audience laughs because they recognize the original and they see how the comedian has taken those real, recognizable features and stretched them to a ridiculous — but entirely logical — extreme.

The primary purpose when someone parodies something is humor. But parodying can also carry a second layer of meaning. By exaggerating someone's features or habits, a parody can quietly — or not so quietly — make a point. If a comedian parodies a politician's long-winded speeches, they might be subtly saying: this person talks endlessly while saying very little. The laughter carries the critique. That said, not every parody carries a serious message. Sometimes it's done purely for fun, with no deeper point intended at all.

Almost anything — a celebrity, a politician, a genre of music, a film, a famous speech, a style of writing, a TV show, or an advertisement. The only real requirement is that the original is recognizable to the audience. A parody of something completely unknown would fail, because people wouldn't know what was being imitated or exaggerated. The humor depends entirely on that moment of recognition: oh, I know exactly what they're making fun of.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words seem close in meaning, so understanding the differences sharpens your understanding of the word considerably.

To imitate simply means to copy someone or something. There is no exaggeration or humor required. A student who imitates a skilled author's writing style to learn is not parodying anyone — they're just studying and copying.

To mock means to make fun of someone, often in a mean or disrespectful way. Mocking doesn't require imitation at all — you can mock someone with dismissive words or cruel laughter alone. Parodying, by contrast, always involves imitation of the original.

To satirize is broader. Satire uses humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize people, institutions, or society — but it doesn't have to imitate a specific original work. A novel that uses absurd fictional situations to criticize a corrupt government is satire. A novel that specifically imitates and exaggerates another famous novel is parody. Parody is often a form of satire, but satire is not always parody.

To spoof is very close to parody and many people use the two words interchangeably. A spoof tends to be lighter and more purely playful, without the critical edge that a parody sometimes carries. In casual speech, the distinction rarely matters.

To caricature means to exaggerate a person's features — usually their physical appearance or personality traits — often in a drawing. It focuses narrowly on exaggerating specific features of a person, rather than imitating a whole work, style, or genre the way parody does.
A Nuance Worth Knowing: Affection, Not Just Mockery

Parodying something does not always come from disrespect or contempt. Many parodies are made by people who deeply love and admire the original. The humor comes from a place of deep familiarity and even warmth. A musician who parodies a genre they adore knows it so intimately that they can perfectly recreate it while gently teasing its clichés. This is why a well-crafted parody can feel affectionate rather than cruel. It is, in a way, a tribute disguised as a joke.

The verb appears in many natural contexts: "The comedian parodied the president's speaking style to great effect." "The film parodies the classic spy genre by making the hero completely clumsy and fearful." "She parodied the fashion industry in her short video." "The song parodies a famous pop hit by replacing its romantic lyrics with lyrics about grocery shopping."

To parody something is to imitate it in an exaggerated, humorous way — to make people laugh and sometimes to comment on the original's quirks or flaws. The audience must recognize the original for it to land. The formula, if you want one, is simply: recognizable imitation + exaggeration + humor.
11741:
Parole is the conditional early release of a prisoner from jail or prison, before they have finished serving their full sentence. "Conditional" is the key word here — it means the person is not completely free. They are let out, but only under a strict set of rules that they must follow. If they break those rules, they go back to prison.

Think of it this way: a person is sentenced to 10 years in prison. After serving 6 years, the authorities decide they have shown good behaviour and seem ready to re-join society. They are released on parole — out of the prison building, but still under the supervision and control of the law for the remaining period.

Parole is not automatic. A group of officials called a parole board reviews each prisoner's case. They look at things like:

  • How the prisoner has behaved inside prison
  • Whether the person shows genuine remorse for their crime
  • How likely the person is to commit another crime if released
  • Whether they have a stable place to live and possibly a job lined up

Based on this review, the parole board either grants parole (approves the release) or denies parole (keeps the person in prison). A prisoner can be denied parole multiple times, meaning they must stay and keep waiting for another review.
The Conditions: What It Means to Be "On Parole"

When a person is released on parole, we say they are on parole. This is a supervised period of freedom. It comes with a list of conditions — rules they must strictly follow. These conditions vary by case, but common ones include:

  • Reporting regularly to a parole officer — a designated official who monitors them and checks that they are following the rules. The parolee (the person on parole) might need to visit this officer weekly, or check in by phone or app.
  • Not committing any crimes — even a minor offence can be enough to send them back.
  • Staying within a certain area — they usually cannot move to another city or region, or travel abroad, without permission.
  • Not associating with other known criminals — they may be forbidden from spending time with people who have a criminal history.
  • Passing drug and alcohol tests — if their original crime was linked to substance abuse, they may be tested regularly.
  • Maintaining employment or attending rehabilitation programmes — they may be required to show they are working towards a stable life.
  • Wearing an electronic ankle monitor — in many cases, their physical location is tracked at all times.

The parolee must satisfy all these conditions for the entire parole period. The moment they violate any condition, their parole can be revoked — cancelled — and they are sent back to prison.

The length of a parole period depends on the original sentence and the laws of the country or state. Generally speaking, the supervision lasts until the point when the original sentence would have ended anyway, or until the parole board is satisfied the person is stable and no longer needs monitoring. At that point, the person is fully free, with no further obligations to the parole system.
A Critical Distinction: Parole vs. Probation

These two words are often confused, and it is worth being very clear about the difference.

  • Parole comes after prison. The person has already been in prison for some time and is released early. They are being supervised instead of completing the rest of their prison term.
  • Probation is instead of prison. A judge decides that, rather than sending a convicted person to prison at all, they will be placed under supervision in the community. They never go to prison in the first place (or their prison time is very short), and they must meet conditions similar to parole.

In short: probation replaces prison; parole follows it.
Parole vs. Simply Completing a Sentence

When a prisoner finishes their full sentence — every single day — they walk out of prison as a completely free person with no ongoing obligations to the authorities (beyond the permanent marks on their criminal record). This is sometimes called being released unconditionally.

Parole is different. It is an early release, and freedom comes at the price of continued supervision and restrictions. The law still has a hold on the person until the parole period ends.

• "Granted parole" — the parole board approved the early release.
    "He was granted parole after serving half his sentence."
  • "Denied parole" — the board said no; the person stays in prison.
    "She was denied parole for the third time."
  • "On parole" — currently serving the supervised release period.
    "He is not allowed to leave the state — he's on parole."
  • "Parole violation" — breaking one or more of the conditions of parole.
    "A parole violation sent her straight back to prison."
  • "Parole officer" — the official assigned to supervise someone on parole.
  • "Parole board" — the panel of officials who decide who gets parole.
  • "Up for parole" — eligible to be considered for parole.
    "He'll be up for parole next year."
A Secondary Meaning: The Military Sense

In military and historical contexts, parole has a related but separate meaning. It refers to a formal promise made by a prisoner of war to their captors. For example, a captured soldier might be released from a prisoner-of-war camp after giving their word of honour (their "parole") that they will not take up arms against that enemy again, or that they will return to captivity under certain agreed conditions. This meaning is rooted in the idea of a solemn spoken pledge.

This military meaning is rarely encountered in everyday modern life, but you may come across it in history books or war literature. The connecting thread between both meanings is the idea of conditional release based on a promise or obligation — you are let go, but you are bound by a commitment.

Parole is a tool that allows the criminal justice system to release prisoners early while keeping them under a watchful eye. It serves two purposes: it rewards and incentivises good behaviour in prison, and it allows the transition back into society to happen gradually, with support and monitoring, rather than all at once. It is not a free pass — it is freedom on a leash, and the leash snaps back the moment the rules are broken.
11742:
A paroxysm is a sudden, intense burst or fit of something — an emotion, a physical symptom, or an activity — that erupts with great force, usually without much warning, and then passes. Think of it like a storm that appears from almost nowhere, hits hard, and then fades away.

The "something" that bursts can be a feeling (like rage or grief), a physical reaction (like coughing or pain), or even a flurry of action. What makes it a paroxysm and not just a regular feeling or reaction is the combination of three things happening together: it comes on suddenly, it is intense, and it is relatively brief (an episode, not a permanent state).

The word lives comfortably in two places: everyday emotional language, and medical language.

1. Emotions and Behavior

In everyday use, a paroxysm describes a violent, uncontrollable outburst of emotion or behavior. The emotion doesn't build gradually — it explodes.

  • She was seized by a paroxysm of grief when she heard the news.
  • He erupted into a paroxysm of rage, throwing his chair across the room.
  • The comedian's joke sent the audience into paroxysms of laughter.

Notice that last example uses the plural — paroxysms — which is common when describing repeated waves of the same intense feeling (fits of laughter that keep coming in bursts, for instance).

2. Medicine and the Body

In medical language, a paroxysm refers to a sudden attack or sharp flare-up of a disease symptom — something the patient's body does abruptly and intensely, often outside their control.

  • The patient suffered a paroxysm of coughing that lasted nearly a minute.
  • She experienced a paroxysm of pain in her chest.

Here, the word signals that the symptom wasn't a dull, steady ache — it was a sharp, sudden, forceful episode. Doctors may also use it to describe a sudden recurrence of a condition that had temporarily quieted down.

To call something a paroxysm, it needs all three of these qualities. Remove one, and the word no longer fits perfectly:

1. Suddenness — It strikes without a long buildup. It catches you or observers off guard. A feeling that slowly grows over days is not a paroxysm. A feeling that ambushes you in an instant can be.

2. Intensity — It is not mild or moderate. A paroxysm of anger is not mild irritation. A paroxysm of coughing is not a quiet throat-clear. The force of it is what makes it remarkable and worth naming separately from ordinary experiences.

3. It passes — A paroxysm is an episode, a fit, a burst. It is not a permanent condition. This is why the word implies something that the person goes through and eventually comes out the other side of. This is also why "paroxysms" (plural) is so natural — these episodes can repeat, hitting in waves.

"Paroxysm" carries a sense of something beyond ordinary control. When you use it, you are saying that the person or body didn't simply choose to feel or react that way — they were overtaken by it. It suggests being seized, gripped, or overwhelmed.

This is why the word is often paired with verbs like:

  • seized by a paroxysm
  • gripped by a paroxysm
  • overcome with / overwhelmed by paroxysms
  • thrown into paroxysms

These phrases all point to the same idea: the person didn't invite it. It arrived and took over, however briefly.

It helps to draw clear borders around the word:

  • It is not a slow, gradual feeling. Sorrow that deepens over weeks is not a paroxysm. A sudden, convulsive wave of sobbing is.
  • It is not mild. You would never say a paroxysm of mild discomfort. The word demands intensity.
  • It is not permanent. A lifelong condition is not a paroxysm. A flare-up of that condition is.
  • It is not casual or everyday. You wouldn't say a paroxysm of hunger before lunch. The word is reserved for things with real emotional or physical weight.

"Paroxysm" is a formal and literary word. You will see it most in:

  • literary fiction and serious prose
  • medical and scientific writing
  • journalism describing dramatic events or reactions

It is rarely spoken in casual conversation. If someone uses it in everyday speech, they are almost certainly being deliberately expressive or emphatic — perhaps even slightly dramatic. In writing, it signals seriousness, precision, and careful word choice. It elevates what it describes.
A Quick Mental Image to Lock It In

Imagine a person sitting quietly. Then, without warning, something triggers them — and they are swept up in an uncontrollable fit of sobbing, or rage, or coughing. They shake, they can't stop, it's powerful and raw. Then, after a minute or two, it subsides. They are back to themselves, maybe a little shaken.

That episode — sudden, intense, and passing — is a paroxysm.
A paroxysm is a sudden, violent, and brief burst or fit of an emotion, physical symptom, or reaction — something that strikes hard, overwhelms for a moment, and then passes.
11743: The word parquet (noun) has two main meanings in English. The first is far more common; the second appears mostly in the context of theatres.
Meaning 1: A Type of Decorative Wooden Floor

This is what most people mean when they say "parquet." It refers to a floor made from small pieces of wood fitted together in a geometric pattern — not just plain planks running in one direction, but an arranged design, almost like a wooden mosaic.

What makes it "parquet" and not just a "wooden floor"?

A regular wooden floor is simple: long planks laid side by side, all running the same way. A parquet floor is different — the short pieces of wood are cut and placed deliberately to create a repeating visual pattern. The pattern is the defining feature. Without the pattern, it's just wood flooring. With the pattern, it becomes parquet.

What do these patterns look like?

The most famous parquet pattern is called herringbone — rows of rectangular blocks placed at 90-degree angles to each other, creating a zigzag effect that resembles the bones of a fish (hence the name). Another very common one is the chevron, which looks like a continuous series of V-shapes or arrows pointing in one direction. There are also basket-weave patterns (which look like woven strips), brick patterns, and many others.

What is it made of?

Parquet is made from hardwood — sturdy, dense wood that can handle foot traffic without wearing out quickly. Common choices include oak, walnut, maple, cherry, and teak. The individual wood pieces used in parquet are small — typically short rectangular blocks or strips — and they are carefully assembled flat on the floor, either glued down, nailed, or interlocked.

Where do you find parquet floors?

Historically, parquet was a mark of wealth and craftsmanship. You'd find it in European palaces, grand ballrooms, and stately homes — the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, for example, has parquet floors. Today, parquet is widely used in upscale homes, hotels, restaurants, and office spaces around the world. It is prized because it is both beautiful (the pattern adds visual richness and elegance) and durable.

Parquet vs. other wood flooring — a quick distinction:

  • Hardwood plank flooring: Long, straight planks, all running parallel. Simple and clean-looking.
  • Parquet flooring: Short pieces arranged in a deliberate pattern. More decorative and complex-looking.

Both are "wooden floors," but parquet is specifically the patterned kind.

In everyday language, how is the word used?

You'd hear or read things like:

  • "The old mansion had beautiful parquet throughout the hallways."
  • "They decided to install parquet in the living room for a more classic look."
  • "The parquet was made of dark walnut arranged in a herringbone pattern."
Meaning 2: A Section of Seating in a Theatre

In the context of theatres, "parquet" refers to the ground-level seating area — the main floor of an auditorium, closest to the stage and below any balconies or galleries above.

Think of a traditional theatre or opera house with multiple levels. The lowest level, where the audience sits on the same floor as the stage (though slightly lower or level with it), is historically called the parquet. Above it might be the dress circle, the upper circle, and the gallery.

In American theatre terminology, this area is more often called the orchestra (or "orchestra stalls" in British English). "Parquet" as a theatre term is older and somewhat formal; you'll encounter it more often in historical writing or in descriptions of 18th- and 19th-century European theatres.

You might see it used like:

  • "They had seats in the parquet, just a few rows from the stage."
  • "The parquet was packed on opening night."

The reason these two meanings share the same word is almost certainly visual: the ground floor of old theatres often had decorative wooden parquet flooring — so the floor itself gave the seating section its name.

What it is
Primary meaningA decorative wooden floor made of small pieces of wood arranged in a geometric pattern
Secondary meaningThe ground-floor seating section of a theatre

If you encounter "parquet" without any theatre context, it almost certainly refers to the flooring. The floor meaning is the dominant, everyday one — you could go your whole life encountering the word only in that sense and never feel lost.
11744:
Parquetry is the craft of creating decorative surfaces — most commonly floors, but also tabletops and furniture panels — by fitting together small pieces of wood cut into precise geometric shapes, arranged so they interlock and form a repeating pattern. Think of it like a mosaic or a puzzle, but made of wood, and where every piece is a clean geometric form: a square, a rectangle, a triangle, a diamond, a hexagon, or a lozenge (a tilted diamond).

The result is a surface that is both functional and visually striking — a floor you can walk on that also looks like a piece of art.

The word specifically refers to work that uses geometric patterns — not pictures, not flowers, not landscapes. Just shapes. Repeating, interlocking, mathematically precise shapes arranged across a surface.

This is the single most important thing to understand about parquetry: it is always geometric. If you see a wooden floor with a repeating pattern of diamonds, or a chess-board arrangement, or a herringbone layout of rectangular planks — that is parquetry.

Wood is the traditional material, and it is almost always different species of wood used together. This is deliberate. Different tree species have naturally different colours — pale ash, golden oak, deep walnut, reddish cherry, near-black ebony, creamy maple. By cutting these different woods and placing them side by side, the craftsperson makes the geometric pattern visible through colour and grain contrast, without needing any paint or dye.

Sometimes the pieces are also cut so that the wood grain runs in different directions between adjacent pieces. Even if two pieces are the same colour, one will appear slightly lighter and the other slightly darker depending on the angle of light — this creates a shimmering, three-dimensional effect even on a flat surface. This is called the chatoyance effect (though you don't need to remember that term — just understand that the pattern can "pop" visually even with a single species of wood, purely through grain direction).

In more decorative work — especially on furniture and decorative boxes — materials beyond wood are sometimes used: tortoiseshell, brass, ivory, mother-of-pearl, or stone. But plain wood remains the most common material.

The craftsperson cuts the wood pieces very precisely using specialist tools, so that each edge is perfectly straight and each angle exactly right. Then the pieces are arranged on a flat surface and glued down — traditionally onto a solid backing (a timber base or, in modern work, a plywood or MDF board). The seams between the pieces fit so tightly that, once finished, you should not be able to slide a piece of paper between them. The surface is then sanded flat and finished (varnished, oiled, or waxed) to protect it and bring out the natural beauty of the wood.

This is slow, painstaking work. A skilled parquetry craftsperson — called a parqueteur — can spend weeks or even months on a single floor for a large room.

Floors are the most common application. If you have ever visited a grand European palace — Versailles in France, for example, is famous for it — or an old manor house, or even a well-appointed hotel or office, you may have seen parquet flooring: a floor made of wooden pieces arranged in geometric patterns, rather than plain planks running in one direction. This is parquetry.

Furniture is the second major application. The flat surfaces of cabinets, chests of drawers, tabletops, writing desks, and decorative boxes are often decorated with parquetry. This was especially popular in 17th and 18th century European furniture, where even small surfaces like the front panel of a drawer might be covered in an intricate geometric wood pattern.

Decorative objects — jewellery boxes, trays, picture frames, even musical instrument cases — may also be decorated with parquetry.

Because parquetry is always geometric, certain patterns appear over and over across history and cultures:

  • Herringbone — rectangular pieces arranged in a zigzag, like the bones of a fish. One of the most recognisable and widely used parquetry patterns for floors.
  • Basket weave — groups of parallel rectangles alternated at right angles to look like woven strips.
  • Brick pattern — rectangles offset like bricks in a wall.
  • Chevron — similar to herringbone but with pieces cut at an angle so the zigzag meets perfectly at a point, rather than stepping.
  • Versailles panel — a more complex square arrangement with diagonals and borders, named after the Palace of Versailles.
  • Diamond and lozenge patterns — square or diamond shapes arranged to create optical illusions of depth or three-dimensionality (like the classic optical illusion of tumbling cubes).
Parquetry vs. Marquetry — A Crucial Distinction

These two words are close enough that people often confuse them, and understanding the difference will sharpen your understanding of both.

Parquetry = geometric shapes, repeating patterns, abstract design. It is about mathematical precision and the beauty of pure form.

Marquetry = pictorial or floral designs. If you see a tabletop decorated with a wooden picture of a bouquet of flowers, or a landscape, or a portrait — using different coloured woods cut into the shapes of petals, leaves, and stems — that is marquetry, not parquetry.

The easy way to remember: parquetry = patterns; marquetry = pictures.

Both involve fitting together small pieces of wood, and the cutting technique is similar — but the purpose and output are very different.

Parquetry is admired for several reasons:

  1. Skill — Cutting dozens or hundreds of small pieces to exact angles and fitting them together perfectly requires years of practice.
  2. Durability — A well-laid parquet floor, when properly maintained, can last centuries. Many floors in old European palaces are hundreds of years old and still in use.
  3. Natural beauty — The patterns are made entirely from the natural colour and grain of wood, with no artificial colouring needed. This gives parquetry a warmth and depth that painted or printed surfaces lack.
  4. Optical interest — Geometric patterns can create illusions of movement, depth, and three-dimensionality on a flat surface.

Parquetry is the art and craft of assembling small, precisely cut pieces of wood (or occasionally other materials) into geometric, repeating patterns to decorate floors, furniture surfaces, and objects. It is distinguished from marquetry by its use of abstract geometry rather than pictorial imagery. The contrast between different wood species, grain directions, and colours is what makes the patterns visible and beautiful. It is a traditional craft associated with fine craftsmanship, luxury interiors, and decorative furniture, with a history stretching back centuries across Europe and beyond.
11745:
As a noun, parricide has two closely related meanings, and understanding both together is the key to truly grasping this word.

First, parricide is the act of killing one's own parent — a father, a mother, or both. If someone murders their own parent, that killing is called a parricide. Second, parricide is also the person who commits that act. So the same word describes both the crime and the criminal. Think of it like the word "murderer" and "murder" rolled into one.
Who exactly counts as a victim of parricide?

This is where the word gets a little wider than most people assume.

At its narrowest, parricide refers to killing one's parent. But in a broader, historically and legally recognized sense, it extends to the killing of any close relative — a grandparent, a sibling, an uncle or aunt, or even a spouse in some older usages. The word has also, in certain historical and legal traditions, been applied to the killing of a ruler, a king, or a head of state — someone who stood in a "father figure" role over a people or a nation.

So the safest, most accurate way to understand parricide is this: it is the killing of someone to whom you owe a natural duty of love, loyalty, and protection — most commonly a parent, but possibly a close family member or symbolic father-figure of a society.
How it relates to other similar words

English has several more specific words carved out of the same general idea, and knowing them helps parricide click into place:

Patricide is the killing specifically of one's father. Matricide is the killing specifically of one's mother. Fratricide is the killing of a brother, and sororicide is the killing of a sister. Filicide is the killing of one's own child. Regicide is the killing of a king.

Parricide is the umbrella. It is the broader word that can, depending on context, cover many of these situations — particularly when the victim is a parent. When a writer or a court uses "parricide," they are usually emphasizing the deeply unnatural and morally monstrous nature of turning against one's own flesh and blood or one's most sacred protector, without needing to specify the exact family relationship.
The weight and tone of the word

Parricide is not a neutral, clinical term. It carries enormous moral and emotional gravity. Across history, cultures, and legal systems, killing one's own parent has been considered one of the most horrifying crimes a human being can commit — a fundamental betrayal of the most basic bond in human life. In ancient Rome, for instance, the punishment for parricide was uniquely brutal and theatrical precisely because the crime was seen as a violation of the natural order itself.

When you see this word in a book, a legal document, a philosophical text, or a historical account, the author is almost never being casual. Using "parricide" instead of simply saying "he killed his father" signals that the focus is on the monstrous, unnatural, and society-shaking nature of the act — not just the bare fact of death.
A few examples of how it appears in real use

"The trial of the young man for parricide shocked the entire village, as no one could believe he had taken his own father's life."
Here, "parricide" refers to the act — the crime of killing his father.

"History remembers Nero as, among other things, a parricide — a man who arranged the murder of his own mother, Agrippina."
Here, "parricide" refers to the person — Nero himself, the one who committed the act.

Parricide means either the act of killing one's own parent (or close relative), or the person who commits that act — and it always carries with it the sense of a profound, unforgivable betrayal of the most fundamental human bonds.
11746:
To parry means to skillfully deflect or ward off something coming at you — whether that's a physical blow or a verbal challenge like a tricky question or criticism. The key word here is skillfully. You don't just run away from it. You don't absorb it either. You cleverly redirect or block it so it doesn't land on you with full force.

Think of it like this: someone swings something at you, and instead of getting hit or just stepping aside, you use your own tool, words, or wit to push it away — gracefully and in control.

1. Physical (Literal) — Blocking an Attack

This is the original, physical sense. In combat — sword fighting, boxing, martial arts — to parry is to block or deflect an opponent's strike using a deliberate counter-movement.

It's important to understand what makes a parry different from simply dodging:

  • Dodging = you move your body out of the way. You are passive. The attack misses because you moved.
  • Parrying = you actively meet the attack and redirect or neutralize it. You don't move away; you engage with it and push it off course.

Examples:

  • "The boxer parried his opponent's left hook with a swift raise of his forearm."
  • "The knight parried every sword strike without taking a single wound."
  • "She parried the attacker's arm before stepping back."

2. Verbal / Mental (Figurative) — Deflecting a Question or Criticism

This is the figurative sense, and it's extremely common in everyday language. Here, to parry means to cleverly avoid or deflect a difficult question, an uncomfortable accusation, or a sharp criticism — without directly answering or confronting it.

Just like in combat, you're not ignoring it (that would be dodging), and you're not fully accepting it either. You meet it head-on, but you redirect it — often with wit, a counter-question, humor, or a vague but intelligent-sounding response.

This is a very common move in politics, interviews, debates, and even casual conversations.

Examples:

  • "The politician parried every question about the scandal by changing the subject to the economy."
  • "When asked why she was late, she parried with a joke that made everyone laugh and forget to press her for a real answer."
  • "He parried the criticism by pointing out his accuser's own flaws."
  • "The CEO parried the journalist's tough questions with carefully worded non-answers."
The Defining Quality: Skill and Control

This is the most important thing to remember about parry. It always implies skill, cleverness, and control. It is never clumsy or accidental.

  • A person who panics and fumbles away an attack has not parried it.
  • A person who answers a hard question nervously and incoherently has not parried it.

To parry is to handle something threatening with composure and technique. It carries a quiet sense of mastery — like you've seen this coming and you know exactly what to do.

Understanding what a word isn't can be just as useful as knowing what it is.

SituationNOT a Parry
  • Ignoring something is not a parry. If someone criticizes you and you pretend you didn't hear them, that's avoidance, not parrying.
  • Absorbing a blow is not a parry. If you just take the punch, you didn't parry it.
  • Stumbling out of the way is not a parry. It lacks the deliberate, skilled quality.
  • Directly answering a question is not a parry — that's just answering. A parry sidesteps the direct answer.

Depending on context, parry can carry slightly different flavors:

  • Defensively: "She had to parry his constant criticisms just to get through the meeting." — Here it feels exhausting, like she's fending off a repeated attack.
  • Smoothly/Impressively: "He parried every tough question with remarkable ease." — Here it's almost admirable, showing mastery.
  • Evasively (slightly negative): "The minister parried all questions about the budget." — Here it can imply that he should have answered but cleverly didn't.

So the word can be neutral, admiring, or mildly critical depending on how it's used — context is everything.
A Simple Way to Always Remember It

Parry = Don't take the hit. Don't run from it. Meet it and redirect it — with skill.

Whether in a sword fight or a press conference, that's always what parry means.
11747:
To parse something means to break it down into its parts and analyze what each part means and how they all fit together.

Think of it like a mechanic who, instead of just looking at a car and saying "it's a car," opens it up, identifies the engine, the transmission, the fuel system, and explains exactly what each component is and how it connects to the others. That careful, structured act of breaking something apart to understand it fully — that is parsing.
The Three Contexts Where You'll Meet This Word

1. Grammar (the original use)

This is where the word lives at home. In grammar, to parse a sentence means to go through it word by word (or phrase by phrase) and label what grammatical role each part is playing.

Take this sentence:

"The dog chased the ball."

Parsing it means identifying:

  • The dog → the subject (who is doing the action)
  • chased → the verb (the action itself, in past tense)
  • the ball → the object (what the action was done to)

You are not just reading the sentence — you are dissecting its structure to understand how each piece functions. A grammar teacher parsing a sentence is doing exactly what a surgeon does with anatomy: naming the parts and explaining their roles.

2. Computers and Programming

This is the most common modern use, and it's almost identical in spirit to the grammar sense.

When a computer parses something, it reads a piece of text, code, or data and breaks it down into structured pieces that it can understand and work with.

For example, when you type a web address into your browser, the browser parses it:

  • https → the protocol (how to connect)
  • www.example.com → the domain (where to go)
  • /about → the specific page to open

The browser doesn't just see a jumble of characters — it parses the address by recognizing the structure and extracting meaning from each part.

Similarly, when a programmer writes code, a program called a parser reads that code before running it. It checks whether the code follows the correct rules and breaks it into logical units the computer can execute. If your code has an error, the parser is often what catches it.

3. Everyday, Informal Use

In general conversation, people use "parse" to mean carefully analyze or interpret something, often something that is complex, ambiguous, or confusing.

Example 1:

"Let me parse what you just said."

This means: "Let me take a close look at exactly what you said and figure out what you mean."

Example 2:

"She parsed every word of the contract before signing."

This means she didn't just skim it — she examined it piece by piece with careful attention.

Example 3 (very common):

"I can't parse what he's trying to say."

This means: "I can't break it down into anything that makes sense — it's unclear or confusing to me."
The Thread That Connects All Three Uses

Notice that in every single context, parsing always involves the same two things:

  1. Breaking something into smaller parts.
  2. Understanding the role or meaning of each part.

Whether it's a sentence in English class, a line of code on a screen, or a confusing statement from a friend — to parse is to stop treating something as one whole lump and instead examine its structure deliberately and methodically.

To understand a word deeply, it helps to know what it isn't.

The opposite of parsing is skimming or taking something at face value — reading words without examining their structure or meaning. Parsing demands active, close attention. It's what a detective does with evidence, what a lawyer does with a contract, and what a linguist does with a sentence. It is never passive.

One very useful phrase you'll encounter:

"That doesn't parse."

This means: "That doesn't hold together logically. I can't make sense of it no matter how I break it down."

It's a way of saying something is incoherent or contradictory — not just confusing in phrasing, but structurally broken in meaning. A politician's contradictory statement, a set of instructions that lead nowhere, an argument with a logical gap — these "don't parse."

You see "parse" in...It means...

To parse is to break something into its components and analyze each one. In grammar, you do it to sentences. In computing, machines do it to text and code. In daily life, you do it to complex ideas, tricky statements, or anything that needs careful dissection to be understood. If you ever see "parse" used, ask yourself: "Someone is taking something apart, piece by piece, to understand how it works." That's always what it means.
11748:
Parsimonious means excessively unwilling to spend money or share resources — to a degree that is unreasonable or even mean. It describes someone who holds onto their money (or anything of value) so tightly that it becomes a fault, not a virtue.

Think of a boss who makes millions but refuses to buy his team basic office supplies. Or a wealthy relative who reuses tea bags three times before throwing them out. That attitude — that almost painful reluctance to part with anything — is what parsimonious captures.
The Crucial Distinction: Parsimonious vs. Frugal

This is the most important thing to understand, because these two words are easy to confuse.

Frugal is positive. A frugal person is wise, disciplined, and avoids waste. They don't spend on things they don't need, and we admire them for it.

Parsimonious is negative. A parsimonious person takes that careful attitude way too far — to the point where it becomes selfish, unreasonable, or hurtful to others. There is no admiration here, only criticism.

The line between them is reasonableness. Choosing a cheaper grocery brand? Frugal. Refusing to turn on the heating in winter because it costs money, while your family shivers? Parsimonious.

So when you call someone parsimonious, you are not paying them a compliment. You are pointing out a flaw.

Parsimonious is a formal, literary word with a sharp, critical edge. It sounds almost clinical, which actually makes the criticism feel even more precise and cutting. You would use it in:

  • Formal writing (essays, journalism, literature)
  • Educated conversation where you want to be expressive but precise
  • Describing a character or institution in a pointed way

You would not use it in casual everyday chat — that's where words like stingy, cheap, or tight-fisted live instead. But those words are blunter and less sophisticated. Parsimonious carries more weight and gravity.

While money is the most common context, parsimonious can describe stinginess with anything of value — time, praise, effort, words, warmth, food, or information.

  • A manager who is parsimonious with praise rarely compliments their team, even when the team does excellent work.
  • A writer who is parsimonious with words uses the bare minimum, leaving out warmth or detail.
  • A host who is parsimonious with food serves tiny portions at a dinner party where guests leave hungry.

In all these cases, the meaning stays the same: withholding something to an unreasonable and often mean-spirited degree.

On a scale of "careful with resources" to "outrageously stingy," parsimonious sits near the extreme end. Here is the rough spectrum:

Economical → Frugal → Thrifty → Careful → Stingy → Parsimonious → Miserly

Miserly is perhaps the only word that surpasses it in severity — conjuring images of a Scrooge-like figure hoarding gold coins. Parsimonious is just one notch below that, but it is still a very strong word.
A Special Use: Science and Philosophy

In academic and scientific contexts, parsimonious can carry a neutral or even positive meaning. Scientists speak of a "parsimonious explanation" — one that explains the facts using the fewest possible assumptions. This is actually considered a sign of a good theory.

This idea is also known as Occam's Razor — the principle that simpler explanations are generally better. In this setting, calling a theory parsimonious is a compliment.

However, unless you are reading or writing in a scientific or philosophical context, you can safely treat parsimonious as a negative word.

1. "The parsimonious landlord refused to replace the broken boiler for three winters."
  2. "She was so parsimonious that she calculated the exact cost of every slice of bread before offering any to guests."
  3. "The CEO's parsimonious attitude toward employee wages stood in stark contrast to his own lavish lifestyle."
  4. "The professor was parsimonious with feedback, leaving students guessing about their progress."
  5. "Of all the theories proposed, the most parsimonious one required the fewest assumptions and was therefore preferred." (scientific use)

Parsimonious means being so reluctant to spend money or give anything of value that it goes beyond wisdom and crosses into meanness — and when you call someone this, you are clearly criticising them, not praising them.
11749:
Parsimony means extreme and excessive unwillingness to spend money or use resources — going so far beyond careful budgeting that it becomes a fault.

Think of it this way: there's a spectrum of how people handle money.

Generous → Balanced → Careful → Frugal → Parsimonious

Parsimony sits at the far negative end. It's not just being careful or thrifty — it's being unreasonably tight with money or resources, even when spending would be perfectly justified or even necessary.
What Makes It Different from Just "Being Careful"

This is the most important thing to understand. The word carries a clear negative judgment. When you call someone's behavior parsimony, you're saying they've crossed a line — from sensible saving into something almost irrational or mean-spirited.

A person who skips a restaurant meal to save money is being frugal. But a person who refuses to buy medicine because it costs too much, or who lets guests go hungry rather than spend money on food, is showing parsimony.

The key signal is this: parsimony causes harm, discomfort, or embarrassment — either to the person themselves or to others — and yet the person still won't loosen their grip on resources.
It Doesn't Only Apply to Money

While money is the most common context, parsimony can apply to anything that someone gives out stingily — praise, time, kindness, effort, or words.

For example: a manager who never compliments their team, even when the work is excellent, can be said to show parsimony with praise. A government that barely funds its schools despite having the budget for it is showing parsimony in public spending.

Parsimony has a second, completely separate meaning used in science, philosophy, and logic — and here, it's not a negative word at all. In fact, it's a virtue.

In these fields, parsimony means the principle of choosing the simplest explanation that fits the facts, without adding unnecessary complexity.

This is also known as Occam's Razor — the idea that if two explanations both account for what you observe, you should prefer the simpler one. Scientists call this the principle of parsimony or scientific parsimony.

Example: You wake up and your sandwich is gone. Two explanations:

  • Your roommate ate it.
  • A stranger broke in, ate only the sandwich, stole nothing else, and left no trace.

The parsimonious explanation is the first one — it's the simplest that fits the evidence.

In this context, parsimony means economy of assumptions — don't multiply complexity beyond what's necessary to explain something.

Here are examples covering both meanings so you can see how the word behaves naturally in context:

Everyday/negative sense:

  • "The landlord's parsimony was legendary — he refused to fix the heating even in the middle of winter."
  • "Her parsimony meant she never tipped at restaurants, which embarrassed everyone she dined with."
  • "The company's parsimony with employee salaries led to its best workers quitting."

Scientific/philosophical sense:

  • "The theory was accepted partly due to its parsimony — it explained everything with just two simple assumptions."
  • "In biology, parsimony guides researchers to favor evolutionary trees with the fewest changes."

The word parsimony belongs to a small family:

  • Parsimony (noun) — the quality or behavior itself. "His parsimony was shocking."
  • Parsimonious (adjective) — describing a person or thing that shows parsimony. "She was parsimonious with compliments."
  • Parsimoniously (adverb) — describes how something is done in a parsimonious way. "The aid was parsimoniously distributed."

One last thing worth knowing: parsimony is a formal, slightly elevated word. You won't hear it in casual conversation every day. People in everyday speech usually say "cheapness," "stinginess," or "being tight-fisted." You're more likely to see parsimony in:

  • Formal writing or literary criticism
  • Academic or scientific papers
  • Journalism and commentary
  • Philosophy and logic

When you encounter it, you now know exactly what it means — and in which direction (negative criticism of excessive stinginess, or positive praise of elegant simplicity) the writer is pointing.
